disease_info: Bipolar II Disorder is characterized by a recurrent course of major depressive episodes and hypomanic episodes, without any history of a full manic episode. Hypomanic periods involve persistently elevated, expansive, or irritable mood and increased energy or activity that are observable by others but less impairing than mania, while depressive episodes are often prolonged and functionally disabling. Clinically, patients frequently present during depression and may minimize or even value their hypomanic periods as times of productivity or creativity, leading to underrecognition. It is distinguished from cyclothymia by the presence of full syndromal depression, and from Bipolar I by the absence of manic episodes and generally less severe mood elevation, though suicidality and role impairment can still be substantial.

narrative.stressor: Over the past year, Angelica’s separation from her spouse has intersected with an increasingly demanding workload at her design firm, where she is leading multiple accessibility and high‑stakes product launches. Friends and colleagues had long noticed cycles where she would throw herself into new projects, community mentoring, and elaborate cooking and hiking plans, followed by stretches where she became unusually withdrawn and hard to reach, but these shifts were attributed to her "hustle" and the stress of the separation. About a month before seeking care, an intense period of late‑night design sprints and social overcommitment was followed by a sharp emotional crash; she stopped going to yoga, canceled hikes, and found herself staring at her design files without being able to move projects forward, which strained client timelines and increased tension with her estranged spouse over shared financial and household responsibilities. When her community center coordinator gently confronted her about missing classes and her sister expressed concern that "these lows keep getting worse" since the separation, Angelica agreed to see a psychiatrist to understand why her mood and motivation had become so unpredictable and difficult to manage.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I’ve completely lost interest in the design work and hobbies that usually keep me grounded, and I can’t seem to care about anything right now.”

narrative.stressor: John had managed his IT workload for years by leaning into predictable routines, but over the last several months his small firm took on several new contracts, leaving him responsible for after‑hours server migrations and on‑call support. Coworkers noticed that he would occasionally have bursts of intense focus and enthusiasm, taking on extra projects and staying up most of the night rebuilding systems, followed a week or two later by stretches where he seemed unusually slowed down, let documentation pile up, and started showing up late to client visits. About a month before presentation, after one such "high" period of nonstop planning and new home tech projects, he slipped into a low period where he began missing fishing meetups, neglected his garden, and made several preventable errors at work, prompting a formal warning from his supervisor and anxiety about losing the path to promotion and certification he had been quietly working toward. When a close friend from his angling club commented that his "ups and downs" seemed more than just stress and suggested he might be dealing with something treatable, John spoke with his primary care provider, who referred him for psychiatric evaluation after hearing how his energy and motivation at work had been swinging in recent months.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Lately I feel drained all the time, like I don’t have the energy to get through my workday or even enjoy fishing on the weekends.”

narrative.stressor: Barbara has long balanced her meticulous lab work with structured hobbies and a strict health regimen, but over the past year her husband’s progressive cardiac illness has required increasing caregiving, frequent appointments, and disrupted sleep. During some stretches she would respond by throwing herself into work and home projects—volunteering for extra cases, redesigning lab protocols, and planning elaborate birdwatching trips and garden overhauls—only to be followed weeks later by periods where she could barely keep up with basic household tasks and began quietly neglecting her own medical checkups. About a month before seeking care, after several nights of fragmented sleep while monitoring her husband, she experienced a brief spell of unusually driven productivity at the clinic and at home, which then gave way to a pronounced downturn in mood and motivation; she started calling off from the running club, forgot key steps in quality‑control procedures, and felt increasingly overwhelmed by the contrast between her professional competence and how disorganized she felt managing her husband’s needs. When a colleague noticed her uncharacteristic errors in radiographic imaging and her husband’s cardiologist suggested that her mood swings and exhaustion might be compromising both her health and her caregiving, Barbara agreed—reluctantly—to a psychiatric referral to understand the recurrent pattern of highs and lows that had become impossible to ignore.
narrative.chief_complaint: “My sleep has been all over the place for weeks, and I can’t seem to get any real rest no matter how exhausted I feel.”
